sections.text: Standard deviation tells you how far a typical value in a data set sits from that data set's mean, in the same units as the data. A small standard deviation means the values are bunched near the average; a large one means they are spread out. It is the square root of the variance, which is the average squared distance from the mean.
How is standard deviation calculated, step by step?

Take eight delivery times in minutes: 32, 35, 29, 41, 38, 30, 36 and 33. The steps are: find the mean, subtract it from every value, square each difference, add the squares, then divide and take the square root.

The eight values add to 274, so the mean is 274 / 8 = 34.25 minutes. The differences always sum to zero, which is why they must be squared before they are added. The squares sum to 115.5. Dividing by n - 1 = 7 gives a sample variance of 16.5 and a sample standard deviation of about 4.06 minutes. Dividing by n = 8 gives a population variance of 14.4375 and a population standard deviation of about 3.80 minutes. These figures match the Standard Deviation Calculator's own method: sum the squared differences from the mean, divide, then take the square root.
Should you divide by n or n - 1?

Use the population formula (divide by N) only when your data covers every member of the group you care about, such as every order in a complete list. Use the sample formula (divide by n - 1) when your data is a sample used to learn about a larger group. Dividing by n - 1 is called Bessel's correction. A sample's values sit closer to their own mean than to the true population mean, so dividing by n gives a variance that is too small on average.

A tiny exact check shows this. Take a population of four values, 2, 4, 6 and 8, whose population variance is 5. Draw every possible ordered pair with replacement (16 pairs) and compute each pair's variance. Dividing by n = 2 averages 2.5, half the truth. Dividing by n - 1 = 1 averages exactly 5. The correction makes the variance unbiased; the standard deviation, its square root, is still slightly low on average, a smaller effect that matters little in practice.
What does the 68-95-99.7 rule really say?

For data that follows a normal (bell-shaped) distribution, the share of values within 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations of the mean is fixed. The values below were computed from the normal distribution's error function and rounded to two decimals; the familiar 68, 95 and 99.7 are rounded versions. Chebyshev's inequality, a separate result, guarantees at least 1 - 1/k squared of values within k standard deviations for any distribution with a finite variance.

The rule is a property of the normal distribution, not of standard deviation itself. In our delivery sample, 5 of 8 values (62.5%) fall within one sample standard deviation (30.19 to 38.31 minutes) and all 8 fall within two. With only eight values, that is consistent with a bell shape but proves nothing about it.
How much can one outlier change the answer?

A lot, because differences are squared. Add a ninth delivery that took 90 minutes (a breakdown, say). The mean rises from 34.25 to 40.44 minutes, the sample standard deviation jumps from 4.06 to 18.97, and the coefficient of variation (standard deviation divided by the mean) goes from 11.9% to 46.9%. The median only moves from 34 to 35 minutes. When a few extreme values drive the result, report the median and the interquartile range alongside the standard deviation, or investigate the extreme value before relying on it.
Why does the same mean not mean the same consistency?

Compare the deliveries above with a second route whose times are 34, 35, 34, 34, 35, 34, 35 and 33 minutes. Both routes average exactly 34.25 minutes. The second route's sample standard deviation is 0.71 minutes against 4.06, and its coefficient of variation is 2.06% against 11.86%. A customer promised a 35-minute window would be treated very differently by the two routes even though their averages match.

items: Using the population formula on a sample, which understates the spread, most noticeably for small n.
Quoting the variance as if it were in the data's units. Variance is in squared units (minutes squared here); the standard deviation is in minutes.
Applying 68-95-99.7 to skewed or bimodal data such as incomes or waiting times with a long tail. Use percentiles instead.
Computing a standard deviation of ordinal ratings (such as 1 to 5 survey scales) and treating the gaps as equal.
Using the coefficient of variation when the mean is near zero, where it blows up and says nothing useful.
Reading much into a standard deviation from very few values. With n = 3 the estimate itself is highly uncertain.

All numbers in this article were computed by script from the stated data. The delivery times are made up for illustration and do not describe any real service.
